description: Mean, median, mode, range, data types, bar charts, histograms and normal distribution.
content_html:
Working with Data

Collecting data is only the beginning. Once a psychologist has run a study, they must organise, summarise and display the results in a way that makes patterns visible and allows conclusions to be drawn. Data handling and descriptive statistics are the tools that do this work. They run through every topic in psychology — understanding them unlocks your ability to interpret any study you encounter.

Types of Data

Quantitative data is expressed as numbers. It allows direct comparison and statistical calculation — for example, the number of words recalled in a memory test, a score on an anxiety rating scale, or the time taken to complete a task. Qualitative data is expressed in words or descriptions. It captures meaning, experience and complexity that numbers cannot convey — for example, a participant’s account of what they were thinking during an experiment.

Both types have value. Quantitative data is easier to compare, analyse statistically and replicate. Qualitative data is richer and more contextual but harder to analyse consistently and more open to researcher interpretation.

Primary and Secondary Data

Primary data is collected directly by the researcher for their own study — running an experiment, conducting an interview, carrying out an observation. It is tailored to the research question and provides the most direct evidence, but is time-consuming and expensive to collect.

Secondary data is data collected previously by someone else, often for a different purpose, that the researcher re-analyses. Examples include published statistics, previously conducted studies, or databases. Strength: saves time and resources. Weakness: the data may not perfectly match the current research question, and the researcher cannot control its quality.

Key Fact

Four data types: quantitative (numbers), qualitative (words/descriptions), primary (collected first-hand by this researcher), secondary (collected previously by someone else). Both quantitative and qualitative can be primary or secondary — these are separate classifications.

Descriptive Statistics: Measures of Central Tendency

Descriptive statistics summarise data concisely. The three main measures of central tendency each give a different picture of the ‘average’ in a dataset.

The mean is calculated by adding all values and dividing by the number of values. For example, if five participants recalled 7, 8, 6, 9 and 5 words, the mean is $$\frac{7+8+6+9+5}{5} = \frac{35}{5} = 7$$ words. The mean uses all the data and is sensitive to outliers — a single extreme value can pull the mean up or down significantly.

The median is the middle value when data is arranged in order. If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values. The median is not affected by outliers, making it a better measure of typical performance when extreme scores are present.

The mode is the most frequently occurring value. It is the only measure that can be used with categorical data (e.g. the most common eye colour in a sample) but gives limited information if every value occurs equally often.

Range

The range describes how spread out the data is. It is calculated by subtracting the lowest value from the highest. For the dataset 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, the range is \(9 - 5 = 4\). A large range indicates great variability in the data; a small range indicates participants performed similarly. Like the mean, the range is sensitive to outliers — one extreme value will inflate it.

Key Fact

Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values. Median = middle value in ordered data. Mode = most frequent value. Range = highest minus lowest. Mean and range are sensitive to outliers; median is not.

Displaying Quantitative Data

Data is often displayed visually to make patterns clearer. Frequency tables show how many times each value (or range of values) occurs. A bar chart uses separate bars to represent each category; gaps between the bars show that the categories are discrete. A histogram is used for continuous data (such as ages or heights grouped into ranges), with no gaps between bars because the underlying scale is continuous.

Many psychological variables, when measured in large populations, form a normal distribution. This produces a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve when data is plotted. The key characteristics of a normal distribution are: the mean, median and mode are all the same value (the centre of the curve); the distribution is symmetrical about this central point; most scores cluster around the mean, with fewer and fewer scores as you move towards the extremes.

Intelligence test scores and height are classic examples: most people score near the average, with progressively fewer people at the extremes. The normal distribution is important in psychology because many statistical tests assume data is approximately normally distributed, and because it provides a reference for understanding how typical or unusual any given score is. A score at the extreme tail of the distribution is rare; a score near the centre is typical. This is why psychologists often use the normal distribution as a benchmark when evaluating individual results.
exam_tip_html: Data handling questions appear across both papers, not just in the research methods section — you might be asked to calculate a mean from a table of results in any topic. Always show your working: write the sum, then divide by n. For normal distribution questions, the key phrase is that mean, median and mode all have the same value and the curve is symmetrical. For bar chart vs histogram, the distinction is discrete (gaps, bar chart) versus continuous (no gaps, histogram) — this comes up regularly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Quantitative data is numerical; qualitative is in words. Primary data is collected by this researcher; secondary is collected by someone else. These are separate dimensions — data can be any combination.
  • Mean (sum ÷ n), median (middle value), mode (most frequent), range (highest minus lowest) are the four descriptive statistics you need to calculate. Mean and range are sensitive to outliers; median is not.
  • The normal distribution is a symmetrical bell curve in which mean, median and mode are equal and most scores cluster around the centre. Bar charts suit discrete/categorical data (with gaps); histograms suit continuous data (no gaps).

practice_questions.text:
A researcher collects data on the number of hours students sleep per night. The results for eight students are: 6, 7, 8, 7, 5, 9, 7, 7. What is the mode of this dataset?
A) 6
B) 7
C) 7.5
D) 8
practice_questions.marks: B) 7 [1 mark — the mode is the most frequently occurring value; 7 appears four times]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'primary data'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Data collected first-hand by the researcher themselves, specifically for their own study.' — both elements present.
Secure: Core idea correct — mentions researcher collecting data directly for their own purpose.
Developing: Mentions researcher collecting data but omits 'first-hand' or 'for own study'.
Emerging: Confuses primary data with quantitative data or secondary data.

practice_questions.text: A psychology student records the following scores on a memory test: 12, 15, 10, 14, 11, 13, 12. Calculate the mean and range for this dataset.
practice_questions.marks:
Mean: (12 + 15 + 10 + 14 + 11 + 13 + 12) = 87; 87 ÷ 7 = 12.43 (allow 12.4 or 12).
Range: 15 − 10 = 5.
Mastering: Both calculations correct with working shown.
Secure: Both answers correct, no working shown.
Developing: One calculation correct.
Emerging: Correct attempt at method but calculation error(s).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a bar chart and a histogram, and state when each would be used in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should:
- Bar chart: used for discrete or categorical data; bars have gaps between them to show that the categories are separate (e.g. counts of participants by eye colour, or mean scores per condition).
- Histogram: used for continuous data grouped into ranges; bars touch each other because the underlying data is continuous (e.g. distribution of ages, scores in intervals).
- Distinction: the presence or absence of gaps reflects whether data is discrete (bar chart) or continuous (histogram).
Mastering: Both types defined with correct data type, distinction clear, example for each.
Secure: Both types defined and distinguished.
Developing: One type defined correctly, other partially.
Emerging: Vague or confused.

practice_questions.text: Describe the key features of a normal distribution and explain its importance in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Shape: symmetrical, bell-shaped curve.
- Mean, median and mode all have the same value at the centre of the distribution.
- Most scores cluster around the mean; fewer scores appear at the extremes.
- Example: intelligence test scores or height in a large population.
- Importance: provides a reference for interpreting scores (typical vs unusual); many psychological variables approximate it; assumed by many statistical tests.
Mastering: All five elements present and accurate.
Secure: Four elements present.
Developing: Shape and mean/median/mode equality described.
Emerging: Basic description only.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the use of the mean and median as measures of central tendency in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Mean: add all values, divide by n. Uses all the data. Affected by outliers.
- Median: middle value when data ordered. Not affected by outliers. Best used when extreme values present.
- Mode: most frequent value — not discussed as the focus is mean and median.
- When to use: mean when data is symmetrically distributed with no extreme outliers; median when data is skewed or outliers present.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength of mean: uses all data values, giving the most sensitive representation of the dataset; works well for normally distributed data.
- Weakness of mean: distorted by outliers — a single extreme score can give a misleading picture of typical performance.
- Example: if nine participants score 10 and one scores 100, the mean is 19 — not representative of most scores.
- Strength of median: resistant to outliers; gives a better picture of the typical score when data is skewed.
- Weakness of median: ignores the actual values of scores, only using position — loses information.
- Comparison: choice depends on the data; for normally distributed data use mean; for skewed or outlier-affected data use median.

Mastering: Both measures accurately described, strengths and weaknesses of each elaborated, comparison made.
Secure: Both described, two evaluation points.
Developing: Both described, one evaluation point.
Emerging: One measure described.

knowledge_checks.q: Which measure of central tendency is the most affected by a single extreme outlier in a dataset?
In a normal distribution, which of the following is true?
options: The mean is higher than the median
The mode is lower than the mean
Mean, median and mode all have the same value
The distribution is skewed to the right

knowledge_checks.q: Data collected directly by the researcher for their own study is called _____ data.
The _____ is calculated by subtracting the lowest value in a dataset from the highest value.
Match each descriptive statistic to its definition:
right: Sum of all values divided by the number of values
The middle value when data is arranged in order
The most frequently occurring value in the dataset

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between quantitative and qualitative data?
flashcard_questions.a: Quantitative is numerical; qualitative is expressed in words or descriptions.
Data collected first-hand by the researcher themselves for their own study.
Data collected previously by someone else for a different purpose.

flashcard_questions.q: How do you calculate the mean of a dataset?
flashcard_questions.a: Add all the values together and divide by the number of values.
The middle value when all values are arranged in order from lowest to highest.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the median preferred when data contains outliers?
flashcard_questions.a: Because the median is not affected by extreme values, unlike the mean.
The most frequently occurring value in the dataset.

flashcard_questions.q: How do you calculate the range?
flashcard_questions.a: Subtract the lowest value from the highest value in the dataset.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the shape of a normal distribution?
flashcard_questions.a: A symmetrical bell-shaped curve, with most scores clustering around the centre.

flashcard_questions.q: In a normal distribution, how do the mean, median and mode relate to each other?
flashcard_questions.a: They all have the same value at the centre of the distribution.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a bar chart and a histogram?
flashcard_questions.a: Bar charts have gaps between bars (discrete data); histograms have no gaps (continuous data).

flashcard_questions.q: What does a frequency table show?
flashcard_questions.a: How many times each value or range of values occurs in the dataset.

glossary_terms.definition: Data that is expressed as numbers and can be statistically analysed.
Data expressed in words or descriptions rather than numbers, providing richer detail about experiences and meaning.
Data collected first-hand by the researcher themselves, specifically for their own study.
Data that was collected by someone else for a different purpose and is being used by the current researcher.
Statistics that describe the typical or central value in a dataset: mean, median and mode.
The arithmetic average of a dataset, calculated by adding all values together and dividing by the number of values.
Extreme values in a dataset that are much higher or lower than the rest, which can distort the mean.
The middle value in a dataset when all values are arranged in order from lowest to highest.
The most frequently occurring value in a dataset.
A measure of spread calculated by subtracting the lowest value in a dataset from the highest value.
A table listing each value or range of values and how many times it occurs in the dataset.
A graph using bars of equal width to represent the frequency or quantity for each separate category, with gaps between bars for discrete or categorical data.
A graph similar to a bar chart but used for continuous data, with bars touching to show there are no gaps between the values.
A symmetrical bell-shaped curve in which most values cluster around the mean, with fewer values at the extremes.

hero_image_caption: Descriptive statistics help psychologists summarise and interpret research data clearly.
